comments.author: @exwi-zed533
comments.text: There still needs to be some sort of 'ultimate map' that it adheres to (for both controls and the environment), and somehow implement a best of the best fit(ness) that is acceptable for display. I feel like this hallucinatory problem isn't going to go without some dedicated problem solving - the program needs to define an ultimate game map (for example, the track, for the racing game, how it is laid out in its entirety down to the centimeter). If we ask for controls or model swapping outside of the ultimate game map, it could have a warning saying that you are adding detail away from the main intended ultimate game map, perhaps with a scale on how much it changes the 'main quest' ('THIS MAY ALTER A MAIN QUEST ELEMENT, DO YOU WISH TO CONTINUE?"). I'm excited for this technology but afraid it's going to be stuck in this hallucinatory hell for a while and no one can do anything with it other than having an incredible tech demo. If a lot of it also depends on training data, aren't we currently limited to what exists in videogames already, also? To get any typed experience it would have to exist already as data that was trained... or have some system rapid enough to train a scene quickly (character, foreground, background, other rule elements and interactions). I'm super excited for this tech.

comments.author: @SonyJimable
comments.text: The biggest near term threat to companies like Nintendo are tools that automate the capture of in game assets in existing media and the creation of libraries that can be used in Open Source game engines similar in capability as UE5. The AI is able to consistently port assets with style themes, scale, and physics into Fan-Made games scripted by people with low technical skills required. These fan-made or community made games can be traded on opensource decentralised web3 marketplaces that are also due to launch during 2026... The nature of these marketplaces mean there is no ownership or admin keys to prevent them being used. The quality of games that can be crafted using these tools are near competitive with AAA titles and are likely going to be distributed Free or under 99 cents each. What is more impressive is the framework, deployment solution, and catalogue process reduce the surface area for any malicious or undesirable code so it is very safe and extremely efficient for medium to lower spec systems... From my understanding, the system requirements are also not limited to x86, so RISC-V and other future systems can be supported. 100% of the components used in all areas are Open Source and can be forked if required.

comments.author: @allenhoekstrajr
comments.text:
I think you need to see this from a different perspective to appreciate what this can do. Ignore replacing creator jobs, AI is still centuries away from that regardless of its speed of getting better.
Now, imagine the AI being in control of outcomes and gameplay. What you do in the game will give the AI an immediate ability to alter how the rest of the game is played. Say you're playing GTA with AI, and you kill one of the main characters. The AI would be able to create a new scenario based on what characters and other scenarios are still in play creating an endless amount of ending possibilities. You still have to train AI. So there will always be room for creativity in how it handles these outcomes.
Also, you could have it add functionality of current events, holidays (remember that Knights game on Sega Saturn) real-world weather, and so much more AI could aid in new gameplay experiences.
The question is "How creative can software companies get with AI injection into games?" not "How will AI replace programmers and artists".
